claims.text: Structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature is governed by formation of a single BCC or FCC phase.
The single phase is stabilized by the alloy's high configurational entropy.
High-entropy alloys can contain approximately equimolar refractory principal elements such as W, Mo, Ta, and Nb.
Ni is an example of a principal element in a near-equimolar high-entropy alloy.
In situ TEM or XRD can reveal microstructural evolution and phase formation.
Refractory-metal high-entropy alloys are of interest for high-temperature aerospace and chemical-industry applications.
High configurational entropy increases with increasing temperature.
The temperature-dependent configurational-entropy effect stabilizes a single phase.
Entropy stabilization prevents formation of multiple phases.
Entropy stabilization prevents segregation of alloying elements.
High-entropy nanoalloys will have improved structural and chemical stability at high temperature.
High-entropy nanoalloys will have increased oxidation resistance at high temperature.
High-entropy nanoalloys will have increased fatigue resistance at high temperature.
Conventional single-principal-element alloys may have lower stability and greater degradation at high temperature than high-entropy nanoalloys.
The prediction is restricted to approximately equimolar, multi-principal-element nanoalloys and may not extend to substantially different compositions or microstructures.
The atomic-scale mechanism by which configurational entropy would stabilize a single phase is not fully understood.
Observation of multiple phases or reduced stability at high temperature would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The proposed falsification experiment deliberately selects a composition already predicted to form multiple phases or have reduced stability. If that composition lies outside the approximately equimolar target domain, its behavior cannot falsify the bounded hypothesis; if it lies inside the domain, the design premise conflicts with the hypothesis's single-phase prediction.
TEM or XRD is presented as the intervention leading to the mediator, but it is an observational characterization method and is not specified as a treatment that causes single-phase formation.
